content.thinking:
The samples directory seems empty, which is fine. I'm thinking through the design now: a gnome tinkerer around 1.2 meters tall including the hat, with a whimsical low-poly style—big head, big nose, bushy beard, oversized hat, stubby legs, and chunky hands and boots on a tiny body, using faceted geometry and a warm palette starting with a red-orange hat.

I'm now detailing the full costume and gear: teal hat with brass band and goggles, mustard jerkin, leather apron with pockets, cream beard, pink nose, brown boots, and a backpack stuffed with gadgets like a telescope, spinning propeller, wrench, antenna, gauge, lantern, pipes, gears, umbrella, kettle, and coiled tubing, plus a tool belt. I'm settling on a neutral A-pose with open, chunky three-finger-plus-thumb hands built as simple joint chains to stay within the joint budget, and starting the skeleton with the hip root positioned at about 0.40 on the y-axis.

Working out the overall height plan at roughly 1.2–1.25 meters, placing boots, short legs, a chubby torso, oversized head, and a tall floppy gnome hat up to about 1.25, with exaggerated proportions like a wide head and big flowing beard and nose. I'm defining the coordinate convention (world-space, model facing +Z, mirrored left/right) and beginning to lay out the spine joints from hips up through chest, neck, and head.

Now I'm building the spine as a curved chain of points from hips through the chest, figuring out how many joints and names correspond to the spans between points, then setting up a short neck chain connecting to the head joint with a slight forward tilt.

For the face, I'm thinking about hiding the mouth beneath a mustache and beard like a classic gnome, planning a small jaw piece for the chin and a tiny visible smile tucked between the facial hair.

Now I'm placing the shoulders at roughly ±0.17 on x and 0.66 on y, with upper arm and forearm each about 0.13 long, and sizing the hands fairly large.

Arm lengths roughly match the shoulder-to-hand distance, so the pose stays nearly straight with a relaxed, slightly-out stance; no need for a held tool since the oversized hands are enough, so I'll tuck any wrench into a belt or backpack instead. Now I'm setting up the leg joints, defining hip, ankle, and leg segment positions.

Setting up boot and toe joints...

I'll finish the boot with a hexagonal swept tube from heel to toe, resting flat on the floor, maybe adding a small curled pointed tip for whimsy. For the torso, I'm thinking of a pear-shaped loft or sweep along the spine chain with varying width and height at each station.

Still refining torso cross-section...

For hips, I'm considering adding a lathe-based flared coat hem for a jerkin-style garment.

Now I'm settling on a color palette: a deep red hat with a patch for a tinkerer vibe, mustard tunic, orange coat, and cream sleeves, picking hues that contrast well against each other.

For the backpack, I'm defining a leather pack box sized and positioned on the gnome's back, with a painted wood-grain texture and a flap lid with straps and buckles.

Now I'm planning the gadgets sticking out of it: a diagonal telescope made of brass and leather rings, a rotor propeller hinged on top, a spring-coiled antenna with a dish, a pressure gauge dial on the side, a glowing lantern, a horn, a rolled blueprint tube, a giant wrench strapped on the right, and cog-shaped gears decorating the back.

Beyond those I'm adding a kettle clipped at the bottom, a copper steam-valve coil, dangling keys and a hammer, and a cute touch -- a tiny wind-up key hinged at the center back that could turn. I'm also sketching goggles on the hat brim made of lathed lens rings with a glowing glass effect and a strap sweep.

Still planning the floppy conical hat with a gear-buckled brass band, a bent drooping tip, and working out head/neck proportions to position it correctly on the model.

Now I'm thinking through the face: adjusting neck and head placement slightly lower, then planning big round eyes with dark pupils and catchlights under bushy white brows, plus an oversized nose built from flattened low-poly geometry.

I'm also designing rosy cheek discs, pointy ears poking out from under the hat, curling swept mustache wedges, and a layered beard built from a tapered loft running from the chin down the chest.

For texture I'm adding extruded zigzag tuft layers with a cream-to-gray paint gradient, plus wispy white sideburn hair near the ears. For the face, I'm placing a jaw/chin block under the mustache and a small open mouth gap between mustache and beard to give the gnome a grin.

Thinking through rigging, I'm deciding whether the beard attaches to the head bone or the jaw bone — since jaw movement would clip through the beard, I'll keep most of the beard on the head and let only the small lower lip/chin piece move with the jaw. I'm simplifying the mouth to a dark slot shape sitting between a tiny skin chin wedge and small cream buck teeth for a whimsical look.

Now I'm planning the hands as oversized mittens, with palm shapes plus four finger chains (thumb, index, middle, ring) each with two joints branching off the wrist, giving a slightly curled neutral pose using low-poly capsule shapes for the fingers.

Palms face inward toward the thighs, and I'm positioning the fingers by extending along the arm direction with lateral offsets across the Z axis—thumb on the front side, then index, middle, ring, and pinky spaced out behind it. Next I'm placing the goggles resting up on the forehead.

Now I'm designing the tool belt setup: a buckled belt at the hips with pouches and loops holding a hammer and screwdrivers, plus an apron with a bib and chest pocket for small tools, built as an extruded leather shape offset slightly from the torso.

Still defining torso sweep...

I'll check the previews, then work out sleeves with tapered teal radius, brass cuff rings, and skin-toned hands, plus trouser leg sweeps in trouser color with boots layered over. For decoration I'm planning SVG decals—a stitched patch, a gauge dial with ticks and needle, and similar textures for the hat, apron pocket, and blueprint scroll.

Eyes I'll build as stacked low-poly spheres (white, dark pupil, catch-light), and for the beard I'm combining a sweep shape with scattered card tufts using a cream pointed-tuft SVG for texture, keeping it modest and stylized. I'm aiming for a whimsical low-poly feel—faceted, few-segment spheres with flat shading and cheerful flat colors—and now placing the head joint and center coordinates in world space for simplicity.

Now I'm computing the actual placement geometry: the head sphere's radius and faceting, nose position and shape, and precise eye coordinates calculated so the eye spheres sit correctly on the curved head surface using the sphere equation.

Setting eyes at 0.895 and brows at 0.935 gives a clean 0.015 gap beneath the hat brim. For the goggles, I'll place a strap band at the hat's base (y 0.975) and put the lenses on the front of the cone above the brim at y 1.0.

Now I'm working out the cone's droop using a curved path through several control points, tapering the radius from wide at the base down to a thin tip as it sweeps forward and down.

I'm checking that the hat cone's radius at each height stays larger than the head's radius there, so the hat fully encloses the head without clipping — it checks out at the base, middle, and top. Total figure height lands around 1.3 meters, which feels reasonable for a gnome.

Now I'm setting up the hat as its own bone chain off the head joint so the tip can flop naturally, with a brim lathe and a small bell or gem at the point. For the ears, I'm planning pointy leaf-shaped extrusions sticking out from the sides under the brim, angled outward and slightly back.

Next I'm sketching the ear leaf outline with a sharp tip flick, thin bevel, and a smaller proud inner-ear extrusion for contrast. Then I'm moving to the backpack, adding a "pack" joint under the chest for the box body and a hinge joint for the lid.

I'm checking the pack's position relative to the torso so it clears the back surface, adjusting its depth and center-z so the front face doesn't intersect the torso, and considering using a bevelled extruded rectangle for a rounded box shape instead of a plain cube.

Now I'm placing gadgets on the pack's back face: a propeller mast rising from the top-center with a hinged hub, plus three radially twisted blades.

Lowering the hub to y 0.9 with a shorter mast and reducing blade radius to avoid clipping the hat, though it still just grazes the head. I'm reconsidering the layout for more visual interest—keeping the propeller centered up top but adding an asymmetric element like a telescope angled up-left-back.

Placing a telescope pack on one side and an antenna with spiral coil and dish on the other for balance, then adding a glowing lantern on the left and a strapped wrench and hammer on the right, plus a pressure gauge for the back.

For the back face, I'm laying out a gauge with copper pipes leading to a gear hinge, considering a wind-up key, and deciding whether to add a horn/funnel shape on the lid before settling on positions for everything.

Instead I'll skip the blueprint tube idea since it conflicts with the mast, and place a rolled bedroll-style scroll across the bottom of the pack with strap and red seals, plus a small copper kettle hanging off the lower right side. I'm also planning side pouches on the pack with tools like a screwdriver sticking out.

Now I'm figuring out the shoulder straps running from the pack over the torso to a chest buckle, tracing the path from the pack top over the shoulder down to the belt, draping it onto the torso surface. I need the torso mesh to widen slightly at the upper chest so the straps sit naturally at the shoulders, with the neck area covered by the head and beard.

Setting the torso's radius profile from hip to neck, then adding small pauldron-like shoulder caps where the sleeves begin. I'm defining the arm joint chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist, then sleeve geometry tapering down to cuffs, with hand geometry attached at the wrist joint.

Now I'm setting up helper functions and pruning imports before writing the actual skeleton code with coordinates and colors.

Setting up the hips joint and spine chain, using a catmull-rom path through four points to build three connected spine segments with proper parenting.

Continuing upward, I'm adding the neck joint parented to the chest, then head and jaw joints with specific pivot points and aim directions so the jaw hinges naturally toward the chin.

I'm noting the head bottom overlaps the shoulders slightly, which gives a whimsical big-head look with no visible neck -- the beard will cover that seam anyway. Then I'm working out the facial surface geometry using the head ellipsoid equation to place the mouth and nose at specific depths based on their vertical offset from the head center.

Now I'm figuring out the mustache and mouth placement since they risk being hidden by the beard -- I want the mustache positioned above a visible gap where a cheerful open mouth shows through before the beard covers the chin, so I'm adjusting the mouth's dark oval and jaw position to peek out beneath the mustache curls.

For the beard itself, I'm shaping it as a tapering cone that wraps from under the chin down toward the chest, using a sweep path with varying elliptical radii that narrow toward the tip so it looks full near the jaw and comes to a point lower down.

I'll skip extra zigzag tufts and instead add side lobe sweeps and scattered card details, maybe a small brass ring clip on the beard tip for a whimsical touch. For the torso, I'm considering adding a decorative stripe pattern to the tunic paint.

Writing tunic paint logic...

For the arms, I'm setting up shoulder-to-wrist limb coordinates with an elbow bend, then checking the mirroring signs for the x-axis positioning.

Building the arm chain naming convention, then sweeping a sleeve along the chain to the wrist with teal coloring and a brass cuff band near the end.

Now I'm adding a shoulder cap sphere flattened at the joint in tunic color, and defining the hand palm position by offsetting from the wrist along the forearm direction, shaping it as a flattened sphere oriented to sit flat against the wrist.

Setting up finger geometry next, placing four finger bases along the palm edge with varying depth offsets and lengths, each finger built from a short chain of two segments plus a tip curving slightly inward toward the palm.

I'm thinking the thumb should angle outward and down with a slightly thicker radius, and fingers parent to the wrist bone pointing downward along the arm. For a tinkerer aesthetic, I like the idea of fingerless leather gloves -- a brown glove covering the palm sphere with a cuff band, while the finger segments stay skin-toned at the tips.

Now moving to legs: setting up hip and ankle joints with proportional lengths and slight bend chains for knees, then sweeping trouser-colored geometry over the thighs and shins. I'm planning boots as a separate shaft cylinder with a folded cuff rim, plus a toe joint off the ankle so the foot sweep can run from heel to ball to toe for a proper boot shape.

For laces I'll add a brass-eyelet strip down the shaft front, keep the toe-cap a darker shade, and add a cream sole stripe as a flat extruded outline.

I'm extruding the sole shape from a foot-like polygon in the XZ plane, slightly oversized versus the foot, sitting at y 0 to 0.012 so it sinks flush with the hex foot bottom without z-fighting.

Now I'm figuring out the toe region: a leather sphere squashed and tapered into a curled-up pointy toe spike, with a boot-colored tip pointing upward and forward, separate from the sole shape.

For the torso, I'm adding a belt as a closed loop around the spine near the hip area, swept with a brown tube, raised slightly to avoid clipping into the legs or hips, plus a brass buckle box positioned at the front using a surface ray to find the correct placement.

Now I'm working out the loop parameterization: angle 0 faces front toward world +Z, and increasing t sweeps counterclockwise around +Y, so t=0.25 is left side, 0.5 is back, 0.75 is right. I'm placing pouches at the front-left and front-right (t≈0.08 and 0.92) and a hammer loop on the left side (t=0.25), using the loop's point and the skin surface's nearest normal to orient each attachment correctly. Next I'm moving on to the apron's bib and pocket details.

For the apron, I'm trying lofted stations from ray hits against the body at decreasing heights with varying widths, but I realize a flat loft would float off the belly's curved sides since the torso surface drops away from center. I'm considering instead building the apron as a membrane stretched between two draped edge curves so it follows the body's contour properly.

Actually, simpler: skip the geometric sweep entirely and just paint the apron directly onto the tunic surface using a region test, giving it a leather color and stitch-line edges, then stick on small 3D bits like pocket flaps for depth—that whimsical hand-painted approach fits better. I'd apply the same trick for suspenders.

Writing apron shape logic...

I'll add a darker leather pocket box with visible tool handles poking out—screwdrivers, a pencil, pliers—plus a smaller chest pocket holding spanner heads. Then I'm shifting to building the torso geometry as a sweep along the spine chain, starting from the hip width at the bottom.

The dome cap at the hip end extends slightly below the torso path, covering the crotch region so the tunic hem naturally drapes over the top of the thighs. I'll use rounded caps on both ends of the torso sweep and add a flared lathe shape for the tunic skirt hem.

The dome's bottom would peek between the thighs from a low angle, so I should color that region with the trouser hue for y below .33 so it blends as pants rather than torso. For the hem, I'm considering adding small pointed cones around the octagon lathe to create a zigzag scalloped edge.

Instead I'll keep the hem as a painted trim stripe using cream bands with a diamond pattern based on sine of x+z, simpler than extra geometry. Now moving to head details: sphere for skin, pink cheek discs, nose, ears, eyes, brows, mustache, mouth, teeth, jaw, beard, and the gnome hat with a rolled brass cuff band instead of a traditional brim.

Adding hat decal patch and goggles...

Still working out the strap geometry and loop placement around the hat. Then I'm planning the tip detail as a tiny brass bell, and the eyes as layered spheres—white base, dark pupil, small highlight—offset slightly forward for a natural look.

For the brows, I'm sketching bushy arcs from a few control points with tufted spikes, checking the math on head curvature so they sit correctly beneath the brim without clipping into the hat's base ring.

For the mustache I'm sketching a curved sweep outward from the philtrum that curls upward toward the cheeks, using tapered flat-sided segments in white. Then I'm placing small pink cheek discs on the head's curved surface, positioning them outward and slightly forward so they sit naturally on the ellipsoid face.

I realize a cleaner approach is to use a surface-nearest-point function to find exact hit locations on the head mesh, then stick small embedded shapes (like short flat cylinders for blush, spheres for eyes) directly onto those points — this generalizes well for eyes, cheeks, and other facial features. Now I'm moving on to extruding the ears from side-surface hit points.

Writing part helper functions...

For gear shapes I'm planning a function that generates an outline with trapezoidal teeth around a circle, keeping the part count capped around 400-500 since holes aren't easy with simple extrusion, so I'll fake the center hole with a darker disc instead.

For spinning gears, I'm setting up a hinge joint at the gear's center aimed along the correct axis so the part rotates properly about its local spin axis, then moving on to think through the propeller's mast-to-hub attachment.

For the propeller, I'm adding a hinge joint at the hub aimed upward, then looping to create three blades positioned around the hub at different angles. I need the blade's outline oriented so it lies flat in the horizontal plane rather than standing vertical like a fin, which means picking the thickness direction correctly using the cross product of the blade's radial direction and a perpendicular horizontal vector.

To give the blades some pitch, I'm tilting both the radial and perpendicular axes together around the blade's own radial axis by an angle, which keeps the two axes orthogonal while introducing the twist. Now I'm defining the paddle-shaped outline coordinates for each blade.

For the telescope, I'm planning separate tube sections with decreasing radius and brass connecting rings, plus glass elements for the eyepiece and objective lens, positioning the whole thing diagonally across the back so it reads clearly in silhouette from the front.

Adding brass strap clamps near the telescope base, then placing a small antenna on the right side with a tilted mast and a copper coil spiraling around it near the top.

Shaping the dish's lathe profile to close properly without self-intersection, then angling its axis up and back so it faces skyward. Now I'm adding a hanging lantern on the pack's left side with a hook, a sweeping chain link, and a hexagonal lathe body housing a glowing core.

Working out the lantern's frame details -- a glass cylinder core, top and bottom caps, and vertical support rods -- while rethinking the chain's path from the pack hook down to the lantern's loop. Now turning to a strapped wrench on the right side, sketching it as a single outlined polygon with a rectangular handle and a notched, circular jaw head.

I'll add a small hole disc for a ring, and paint the handle red below a threshold height while leaving the rest steel-colored, then attach the finished wrench to the pack on the right side.

Now I'm figuring out the orientation vectors for the wrench so it lies flat against the pack's side plane, computing cross products to get the correct outward thickness direction and positioning its bottom and top ends along the pack surface.

I'm placing the wrench outside the pack's right edge, tilting it slightly outward so it reads clearly as a separate silhouette next to the shoulder, and considering scaling the figure down a bit to keep proportions clean. I'm also planning additional gear: a hammer on the left belt loop, pliers, and a screwdriver set tucked in a pouch, and now positioning a small pouch box on the pack's left side to hold tool handles.

Resolving positioning conflicts: moving the left pouch higher and hanging the lantern lower from the bottom-left corner so it sits behind the hip, while the telescope goes near the top-left. On the right side, the tall wrench pairs with a kettle hanging at the bottom-right. For the back face, I'm adding a gauge, pipes, gears, a wind-up key, a funnel horn, a valve, plus decorative patches and star stickers, and setting up a hinged lid flap at the top-back edge that swings open and extends forward over the top and front slope.

Working through the lid flap geometry, I'm defining it as a plate extending along the pack's depth and width with its thickness oriented upward, then adding a front drop-over section with a buckle strap and brass lock -- but I'm realizing I should reconsider the hinge orientation, since the flap typically opens from the back of the pack rather than folding toward the body.

I'm placing the hinge joint at the top-front edge and spanning the flap backward over the top then down the back face, attaching a buckle strap with two hanging straps, and planning gauges mounted below. For the body itself, I'm extruding the front-view outline with a bevel and setting up a painted leather material with grain texture.

Now I'm checking placement of the bedroll against the pack bottom and skirt geometry, adjusting the z-center slightly so the bedroll clears the skirt's radius without clipping through it.

I'm also reconsidering scale: the backpack feels too small next to the torso, so I'm oversizing it for a whimsical gnome look, around .44 wide and .38 tall, shifting the wrench accessory accordingly. With the proportions settled, I'm moving on to writing the texture SVGs, starting with the gauge dial.

For the hat patch I'm sketching a small stitched square with a dashed border and a simple star emblem instead of any logo, and adding pointed beard wisps plus rivet details as small merged spheres. I'm also adding a sticker-style badge on the pack showing a wrench-and-cog icon as an original decal, then moving into actually writing the code with care around the API specifics.

Setting up the sweep, rod, and part helper functions, with mirrored left/right loops that flip the x-coordinate by sign, and defining default orientation axes so each geometry's normal lines up correctly when placed on a surface...

For eyes, I'm working out how to flatten a sphere geometry along its normal axis to form a believable eye shape, scaling it before placing it via the stick helper.

For the pupil, I'll stick a smaller dark sphere onto the eye's surface, finding the point nearest the forward direction so it faces outward correctly, and I'm considering whether to keep edges flat for a cuter low-poly look. I'm also starting to think about what accessory kit pieces—lantern, lens glass, goggles—might fit next.

Now I'm sorting out the arm chain: the wrist should correspond to the chain's tip joint rather than a separately indexed joint, so I'll reference arm.tip directly when sweeping the limb geometry. For the torso, I'm planning to sweep along the spine chain with a radius function varying over the path, and I need to decide whether to fold the hips into that same chain or treat them separately.

For items placed with `at` that aren't directly on a chain, I'm defaulting them to the nearest joint, but for most torso decorations I'll explicitly name the bone -- defining chest and belly as specific spine joints so I can anchor things like shoulders and the chest piece precisely along the spine's vertical span.

Now I'm working out the suspender straps draping over the torso, routing them from the pack across the shoulders using rough 3D path points that I'll later snap onto the torso surface with a lift offset so they follow the body's curvature naturally.

I'm giving the straps an elliptical thickness profile across their length and planning brass slider buckle boxes where they cross, plus a horizontal chest strap connecting the two shoulder straps around chest height.

Then I'm working out a smooth torso radius function that interpolates between key width values at different heights—narrower at the shoulders, widening at the belly, tapering again toward the chest and top—so the body silhouette curves naturally rather than being a uniform cylinder.

Now I'm working out the skirt geometry as a lathed shape around the hip bone, defining the outline radius and height points relative to the torso position.

I'm checking the skirt profile doesn't self-intersect and verifying the belly bulge doesn't poke through the skirt top awkwardly, deciding to make the skirt slightly elliptical by scaling the lathed part in z to account for the front torso curve.

I'm figuring out the belt geometry: it needs to be a horizontal closed sweep around the torso at a specific height, using a flat circular cross-section with a few sides so it reads as a thin band rather than a tube.

Next I'm adding a brass buckle up front made from a layered box, then setting up how pack parts attach to bones -- defaulting to the chest joint via a helper function, while a few special pieces (propeller, gears, etc.) get their own dedicated joints since they're wide enough that automatic nearest-joint assignment would pick the wrong bone.

For small repeated pieces like rivets, I'll merge their geometries into single meshes to keep the part count manageable rather than spawning hundreds of individual parts. Starting to write the actual file now -- metadata block, color palette constants, a vector helper, and the skeleton of the build function with the part-creation utility.

Writing part wrapper and geometry helpers...

Adding pupils and tiny highlight spheres to each eye for a cute inward gaze, then starting on the eyebrow curves using catmull paths.

For the brows, I'm checking that the positioning sits just under the hat brim without colliding with the ring geometry. Now I'm shaping the nose from a scaled icosahedron with a flattened profile, embedding it into the face surface and adding a small lighter highlight sphere on its surface.

For the cheeks, I'm placing blush discs by finding the nearest surface point outward from each target position. For the mouth, I'm scaling a sphere into an ellipse shape, orienting it along the face normal, and embedding it with a dark red color plus a tiny pink tongue and two cream teeth boxes just inside it.

The chin gets a scaled sphere blending into skin tone mostly hidden by the beard, plus a small pink lower lip shape, and now I'm positioning the mustache above the mouth to sweep over the teeth area without fully covering them.

I realize the mustache overlaps the mouth and teeth, so I'm redesigning the vertical face layout entirely -- repositioning eyes, nose, mustache, mouth, and teeth to sit in proper stacked order between the brow and chin so nothing collides.

For the beard, I'm planning a gradient from cream to light grey with vertical streak-like stripes to suggest texture, keeping the mustache the same color, and setting up a simple joint chain for the hat attached beneath the head.

The hat chain tapers upward through four segments from the head to a pointed tip near the top, with the radius shrinking from about 0.17 down to zero so the end forms a cone, using flat caps at the base and a rounded taper toward the point.

Adding details: a brass leather band ring around the hat sweep, a square brass buckle with a gear motif at the front, goggles, a mottled red paint pattern for subtle fabric texture, and a tiny brass sphere bell fixed right at the cone's tip point. Now I'm ready to move on to packing everything together and writing the gadgets code, including a wrench, before assembling and running the full file.

input.command: mkdir -p samples scratch/gnomeTinkerer; sed -n 1,80p src/index.ts | head -40; grep -n "flat\|scale" src/builder.ts | head -30; cat kits/glow.ts | sed -n 1,40p
